strengths: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of an underexplored problem: critic staleness in on-policy critique-guided RL, supported by a dedicated qualitative analysis (t-SNE of failure-diagnosis embeddings) that provides concrete evidence for the core motivating claim of failure-pattern drift.

The saturation-aware (SA) gain-shaping reward is a principled and mathematically well-motivated contribution: it is derived as a path integral of a difficulty-weighting function, and the authors explicitly verify desirable properties (additivity/path-consistency, antisymmetry) that give it a cleaner theoretical grounding than an ad hoc heuristic.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across four qualitatively different environments (web navigation, embodied tasks, scientific reasoning, deep search) and two backbone model families (Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-7B), showing consistent improvements over a GRPO baseline under the same training budget.

Ablations (frozen critic, SA-reward removal) directly probe the two central design claims and mostly support them, and the case studies in the appendix make the mechanism (critique generation, refinement) concrete and interpretable.
Method is clearly presented with full pseudocode, prompt templates, and a coherent diagram, which aids understanding and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Compute/sample-fairness of comparisons is unclear: ECHO's cascaded rollout requires N critiques × N refinements per query in addition to the standard GRPO rollout, but it is not clearly stated whether the GRPO baseline is given a matched sampling/compute budget (e.g., same number of total generations or gradient updates), making the reported gains difficult to interpret as arising purely from the proposed synchronization/SA-reward mechanism rather than additional inference-time compute.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the main results (Table 1) or ablations, so it is hard to assess whether the reported improvements (e.g., 7.28-point average gain) are statistically robust versus run-to-run noise, which is a common concern for RL training with LLM agents.

The SA-aware ablation table has missing entries for ALFWorld and DeepSearch (marked '–'), and the paper explains this is because SA shaping needs non-binary/continuous rewards, but this limits generality of the proposed reward design to only two of the four evaluated environments, and the paper does not discuss how SA shaping should be applied (or whether it is applicable at all) in binary-reward or format-sensitive settings like ALFWorld/DeepSearch.

The framework's effectiveness is coupled to the quality/calibration of an external reward model R that scores both baseline and refined trajectories; this dependency (acknowledged in Limitations) is significant since critic and policy co-evolution both hinge on this signal, but no experiments probe robustness to noisy/miscalibrated reward models.

Comparisons against much larger proprietary/open models (GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B) as if peers to a fine-tuned 4B/7B model are somewhat apples-to-oranges and mainly serve promotional framing rather than rigorous ablation of the proposed mechanism; the paper would benefit from being clearer that these comparisons are for context, not primary validation.

Novelty relative to closely related training-based critic methods (e.g., RCO, CTRL) that also optimize critics via refinement utility is incremental; the main differentiators (synchronized/on-policy joint updates, SA reward) are useful but not radically different in framing, and a direct empirical comparison against RCO/CTRL under matched conditions is missing.

Some implementation details relevant to reproducibility (e.g., exact GRPO clipping epsilon, KL coefficient β, number of training steps/epochs, variance in reward-model implementation per environment) are not specified in the main text or appendix, limiting exact reproducibility.

strengths: The central motivating phenomenon—critic staleness under distributional drift of failure patterns during on-policy training—is clearly articulated and directly probed with a dedicated diagnostic study (t-SNE visualization of failure-diagnosis embeddings across training phases), which is a nice piece of supporting evidence rather than pure conjecture.

The saturation-aware reward shaping is mathematically well-motivated, with clean, checkable properties (path-consistency/additivity, antisymmetry) that connect it to established potential-based reward shaping theory (Ng et al., 1999).

The method is evaluated across four qualitatively different environments (web navigation, embodied tasks, scientific reasoning, deep search) and two backbone models (Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-7B), showing consistent relative gains over a GRPO baseline in most settings.
Ablations (frozen critic, w/o saturation-aware reward) are included and generally support the claimed contribution of each component.
The paper is clearly written with helpful figures (training curves, density scatterplots) and includes reproducibility-relevant details (hyperparameters, prompts, pseudocode) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The compute/sample budget of ECHO is substantially larger than the GRPO baseline: each step involves an initial rollout, N critic generations, N conditioned policy refinements, and N+1 reward-model calls, versus a single group rollout in GRPO. The paper claims comparisons are under "the same training budget" but never clarifies whether GRPO is given an equivalent number of total rollouts/reward calls; without compute-matched baselines, the reported gains conflate the benefit of co-evolution with the benefit of simply doing more inference/critique-refinement per query.

The core empirical claim is that existing training-based critic methods (RCO, CTRL, CGI) suffer from staleness, yet none of these directly comparable prior critique-guided RL baselines are actually implemented and benchmarked in Table 1 — only GRPO (no critic at all) and generic strong LLMs are compared. This leaves the paper's central novelty claim (co-evolution vs. static critic) largely unvalidated against the methods it is positioned against.

The saturation-aware (SA) ablation is missing entries for ALFWorld and DeepSearch (marked "–" in Table 2), and the paper states SA reward requires non-binary reward signals — this suggests the proposed reward design is not applicable to at least two of the four evaluated environments, undermining the generality claimed for the framework as a whole.

No variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing is reported for any of the results (Table 1 and Table 2), despite RL training being known to be high-variance; single-run point estimates make it difficult to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., 7.28 average points) are robust or within noise.

The framework's effectiveness is entirely contingent on access to a reliable, fine-grained external reward model R at training time (used both to score rollouts and to compute the critic's saturation-aware reward). The paper's own limitations section acknowledges this dependency but provides no empirical analysis of reward-model quality/calibration, robustness to noisy rewards, or reward hacking risk, despite the co-evolutionary loop plausibly amplifying such artifacts.

The critique-generation prompt (Appendix D) is fairly template-constrained (fixed output format, "at most 1–2 suggestions," explicit instruction to treat the official score as ground truth), which blurs the line between the proposed "adaptive" critic and the template-based critics the paper criticizes in the related work, without a clear ablation isolating how much of the gain comes from critic adaptivity per se versus this structured prompting scheme.

The qualitative case studies (Appendix E) are illustrative rather than systematic evidence; they read as cherry-picked examples of successful refinement rather than a representative or randomly sampled analysis of critique quality/failure modes.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: identifies and empirically demonstrates critic staleness under on-policy distribution shift, a real limitation of prior critique-guided RL methods that rely on frozen/offline critics.

The saturation-aware gain-shaping reward is a principled and elegant design (path-consistent, antisymmetric potential-based shaping) that directly targets the 'equidistant fallacy' of linear reward differences, with supporting analysis (Figure 4, Table 2) showing it concentrates more mass in the reward-improving region near the ceiling.

Extensive empirical validation across four diverse environments (WebShop, ALFWorld, SciWorld, DeepSearch) and two backbone families (Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-7B), with consistent gains over GRPO and additional baselines (RCO, LUFFY) in the appendix.

Thorough auxiliary analyses beyond the main comparison table: t-SNE visualization of failure-pattern drift, frozen-critic ablations, critique granularity evolution, critique-refinement alignment audits, and training-time overhead breakdown, which collectively substantiate the core mechanistic claims rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy numbers.
Reasonably reproducible: full pseudocode, hyperparameters, and prompt templates are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Compute/sample-budget fairness versus GRPO is not clearly established: ECHO's cascaded rollout draws N critiques and then N refinements (up to 2N+1 generations per query) versus GRPO's N rollouts; the paper asserts a modest ~15% wall-clock overhead but does not clarify whether the GRPO baseline is given a matched sample/generation budget, making the core comparison in Table 1 potentially confounded by extra inference-time compute rather than the co-evolution mechanism per se.

The external reward model R, which supplies both the policy training signal and the critic's saturation-aware reward, is never concretely specified (its architecture, source, or reliability), which is a significant reproducibility and soundness gap given that the whole co-evolutionary loop is anchored to this signal; the acknowledged risk of the critic/policy jointly overfitting to reward-model artifacts is only mentioned in Limitations without any mitigating ablation.

All main results, ablations, and RQ-analyses appear to be single-run numbers (no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds) despite training being RL-based and known to be high-variance, which weakens confidence in the reported margins (e.g., the 42% relative DeepSearch gain).

Several qualitative and diagnostic analyses (failure-pattern drift labeling, critique granularity classification, critique-refinement alignment auditing) rely entirely on a single external LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-pro) without any human validation or inter-rater reliability check, raising concerns about circularity and judge bias in supporting the paper's central mechanistic narrative.

Proprietary-model comparisons in Table 1 are not well controlled (different scales, no RL fine-tuning applied to them, and GPT-5 substantially outperforms ECHO on DeepSearch), which somewhat undercuts the framing that ECHO is broadly competitive with frontier models.

The method combines several existing ideas (GRPO, potential-based reward shaping à la Ng et al. 1999, critique-refinement co-training similar to RCO/CTRL) in a new configuration; while the execution and shaping formulation are clean, the conceptual novelty relative to closely related training-based critic works (RCO, CTRL, CGI) is incremental and the paper's main differentiator (synchronization) is validated mainly through one ablation (frozen critic) rather than a deeper comparison against alternative asynchronous-update schedules.
